newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Indonesia's Aceh asylum-seekers riot in Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Aceh asylum-seekers riot in Malaysia.

text.p: More than 50 political asylum-seekers from Indonesia's Aceh province rioted at a Malaysian detention camp on Tuesday to protest against deportation, witnesses said.

Police used tear gas and batons to quell the two-hour long riot at the Langkap camp for illegal immigrants in the north Malaysian state of Perak, before loading the protestors onto five trucks, the witnesses told Reuters at the scene.
They said the trucks were believed to be taking the inmates to Port Klang near Kuala Lumpur, where two Indonesian ships were waiting to take them back.

"They used tear gas. And then the police attacked them (the inmates). All we could hear was their shouts and cries," said Iqlil Tengku Ilias Leube, a Malaysia-based Acehnese businessman who watched the riot outside the camp.
A Reuters journalist at the camp saw two inmates with their heads bandaged being loaded on to a truck.

As the trucks rolled out of the camp, shouts of "Aceh Merdeka" (Free Aceh) from the inmates were heard. Free Aceh is a pro-independence movement that has alleged that asylum-seekers deported to Indonesia are murdered.
The police have declined to comment on the riot and whether it was sparked by the move to deport the protestors.
A police spokesman, Mohd Ghazali Mohd Amin, told Reuters in Kuala Lumpur that he knew of no deportation planned for Acehnese on Tuesday.
"There is no such thing, as far as I know," he said.
His deputy, Shamsuddin Ali, said the last deportation of Acehnese was in June this year, when about 20 Acehnese were sent back.
Hundreds of Acehnese have fled across the Malacca Strait separating the Sumatra island and Malaysia since March, 1992, to escape fighting between the Indonesian army and Aceh Merdeka.
Malaysia has not recognised the Acehnese as political asylum-seekers and has said it will persuade them to return home.
In 1992, as many as 600 Acehnese were reported remanded in Malaysia, together with other Indonesian illegal immigrants who had come to the country in search of jobs.
But police said the numbers may have been reduced now.
"What we have for this year is 12,840 Indonesians in our detention camps, and there's no breakdown of their ethnicity," said another police spokesman.
